name: Papillary tumour of the pineal region
aliases: papillary tumour of the pineal region
papillary tumor of the pineal region
CNS WHO grade 2 or 3 pineal tumour

reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of the CNS
clinicalPearls: A rare neuroepithelial tumour of the pineal region occurring in both children and adults
Presents with features common to pineal masses: obstructive hydrocephalus and dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) signs from tectal compression
MRI shows a well-circumscribed, often partly cystic, enhancing pineal mass
Thought to arise from specialised ependymal cells of the subcommissural organ, giving a distinctive papillary architecture
Histology shows papillary and more solid epithelial-like areas; immunopositivity for cytokeratins (notably CK18) helps distinguish it from other pineal tumours
Behaviour is variable and it has a notable tendency to recur locally despite treatment
Management combines maximal safe resection with radiotherapy considered for residual or recurrent disease
reference.pathophysiology: Papillary tumour of the pineal region is a rare neuroepithelial neoplasm believed to originate from specialised ependymocytes of the subcommissural organ within the pineal region. It forms a circumscribed mass with a characteristic mixture of papillary structures, in which epithelial-like cells surround fibrovascular cores, and more densely cellular solid areas. The tumour cells express cytokeratins, a feature that helps separate it from pineal parenchymal tumours and ependymomas. Grading is imprecise but corresponds to CNS WHO grade 2 or 3, and the lesion is characterised clinically by a marked propensity for local recurrence. Its midline pineal location readily obstructs cerebrospinal fluid flow and compresses the dorsal midbrain.
additionalDifferentials: Pineal parenchymal tumour of intermediate differentiation
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced brain MRI to characterise the pineal mass and hydrocephalus
Craniospinal MRI to evaluate for dissemination
CSF and serum germ cell tumour markers to exclude germinoma
Histopathology showing papillary and solid epithelial-like areas
Cytokeratin (including CK18) immunohistochemistry to support the diagnosis
CSF cytology for staging where appropriate
redFlags: Acute obstructive hydrocephalus with raised intracranial pressure
Progressive dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) signs and impaired consciousness
Features suggesting dissemination along the neuraxis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is intermediate and difficult to predict, being limited chiefly by a high rate of local recurrence even after resection and radiotherapy. Extent of resection influences outcome, and long-term surveillance is required because recurrences may occur years after initial treatment.
pitfalls: Misclassifying it as an ependymoma or pineal parenchymal tumour without cytokeratin staining
Underestimating the strong tendency to local recurrence and relaxing surveillance
Overlooking a coexisting germ cell tumour by not checking tumour markers
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
Louis DN et al. The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System
